lines: Lecture two. Why do we need evolutionary algorithms? Optimisation, and hardness.
Take three items, and aim for a total of one hundred kilograms.
Each item is a bit. A one takes the item, and a zero leaves it.
The fitness, f of s, is how far we are from one hundred. Smaller is better.
Exhaustive search means trying every subset.
We try all eight. A hundred and ten is the best, with f equal to five.
Three items make eight possible solutions.
Each extra item doubles the count.
A real water network has twenty-one pipes, with sixteen sizes each.
Trying every design would take six hundred million years.
Here is a tiny exponential, next to a polynomial.
At n equals forty-four, the exponential overtakes.
Now a real run, with a bigger exponential.
Microseconds for the polynomial. Years for the exponential.
Connect all five towns as cheaply as possible.
Prim's method: take the cheapest cable to a new town.
Keep adding the cheapest cable, with no loops.
It is fast, and always optimal. This is an easy problem.
Now add a new rule: at most two cables per town.
But the best tree has three cables at C.
Run the same greedy method again.
An early cheap choice blocks cheaper ones later.
Greedy gets twenty, but a tree costing nineteen exists.
Nearest neighbour gives an instant, decent tour.
The evolutionary algorithm starts from random tangles.
It keeps improving its best tour.
Given time, it overtakes the quick method.
This is approximate: good answers, but no guarantee.
Here is a population of ten solutions, each with a fitness.
Select: the fitter ones are more likely, not only the best.
Vary: the children can be better, or worse.
So next: who stays?
Replace everyone, and the old best can be lost.
Merge, and keep the best ten, so the best survives.
Or replace the weakest, and the best survives too.
Then we repeat the loop.
Remember: trying every solution is too slow, because the work grows exponentially.
Greedy methods are fast, but they can get stuck.
An evolutionary algorithm gives good answers in reasonable time.
